title: India Achieves Landmark 300 GW Non-Fossil Fuel Power Capacity
body_text:
In a major milestone for the nation's clean energy transition and climate action targets, India has crossed 300 GW of non-fossil fuel-based installed electricity generation capacity as on 31 st July, 2026; over 60% of the 500 GW capacity targeted to be achieved by 2030.
Breakdown of Non-Fossil Fuel Capacity (as on 31.07.2026):
Solar Power: 164.59 GW Wind Power: 58.14 GW Hydro Power (Large & Small): 57.24 GW Bio-power: 11.75 GW Nuclear Power: 8.78 GW
Total Non-Fossil Capacity: 300.50 GW
The share of non-fossil fuel electricity capacity in the country’s total electricity generation capacity (which is around 552 GW at present), has reached over 54%.
Backed through the key policy enablers provided by the Government for this transformation, this monumental achievement highlights India’s rapid progress towards building an Aatmanirbhar energy ecosystem and securing the target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.
The growth in clean energy generation has been anchored by stellar contributions across sectors. Solar energy remains the key growth engine with around 165 GW at present from just 2.8 GW in 2014.  Concurrently, the wind energy sector has also seen strong momentum reaching to over 58 GW from 21 GW in 2014.
During 2025-26, a record capacity of 55.29 GW non-fossil fuel based electricity capacity was installed in the country with key contributions from 44.6 GW solar power and 6 GW wind power.
The rapid progress in renewable energy capacity is also reflected in renewable energy generation in the country which has increased from 190.96 billion units in 2014-15 to 477.79 BU in 2025-26.
To support this rapid expansion and ensure supply chain independence, India has transformed its domestic manufacturing capabilities. Driven by the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme focusing on the nation's solar installations with high-efficiency, indigenously produced modules, the enlisted capacity under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) for Solar PV Modules has crossed the historic 200 GW milestone, rising from just 2.3 GW in 2014.
Clean energy transition is no longer just a climate commitment—it is central to shaping India's industrial competitiveness, energy independence, and economic resilience.
The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy is also driving deep industrial decarbonization, positioning India to become a global hub for the production, usage, and export of Green Hydrogen and its derivatives, through the implementation of the National Green Hydrogen Mission.
****
Nihi Sharma/ Laxya Lohan

ministry.name: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy

enrichment.summary: India has crossed 300 GW of installed non-fossil fuel electricity generation capacity as on 31 July 2026, comprising 164.59 GW solar, 58.14 GW wind, 57.24 GW hydro, 11.75 GW bio-power and 8.78 GW nuclear power. This represents over 60% of the 500 GW non-fossil capacity target for 2030 and over 54% of India's total installed capacity of around 552 GW. A record 55.29 GW of non-fossil capacity was added in 2025-26 alone, and domestic solar module manufacturing capacity under the ALMM list has crossed 200 GW.
enrichment.context:
India's non-fossil fuel capacity target of 500 GW by 2030 is part of its enhanced Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement, announced at COP26 in 2021 as part of the 'Panchamrit' commitments, which also include achieving net-zero emissions by 2070 and meeting 50% of energy requirements from renewable sources by 2030. Key policy enablers behind this growth include the PM-KUSUM scheme for solar in agriculture, PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana for rooftop solar, the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for high-efficiency solar PV modules, the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) to promote domestic manufacturing and reduce import dependence (especially on China), and various solar/wind park schemes. Nuclear power's relatively modest 8.78 GW share reflects long gestation periods for nuclear projects, though India has been pushing amendments to the Atomic Energy Act and Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act to attract private investment.

This milestone is significant not just for climate commitments but for energy security, given India's heavy dependence on imported fossil fuels for its energy basket. It also ties into the broader push for domestic manufacturing self-reliance ('Aatmanirbhar Bharat') in solar equipment, reducing historical reliance on imported panels and cells. The mention of the National Green Hydrogen Mission signals the next phase of India's energy transition strategy, aiming to decarbonize hard-to-abate industrial sectors like steel, fertilizers, and refining, while positioning India as an export hub for green hydrogen and its derivatives like green ammonia.

prelims_questions.question: As per the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy's data (as on 31 July 2026), which of the following non-fossil fuel sources contributes the largest share to India's installed capacity?
prelims_questions.explanation: According to the release, Solar Power accounts for 164.59 GW out of the total 300.50 GW non-fossil capacity, making it the largest contributor, followed by Wind (58.14 GW) and Hydro (57.24 GW).

prelims_questions.question: India's target of achieving 500 GW of non-fossil fuel-based electricity capacity by 2030 was announced as part of which international commitment?
prelims_questions.explanation: India announced the 500 GW non-fossil fuel capacity target by 2030, along with other climate goals collectively called 'Panchamrit', at the COP26 summit in Glasgow in 2021.

mains_questions.question: India has achieved 300 GW of non-fossil fuel-based electricity generation capacity, surpassing 60% of its 2030 target. Discuss the key policy interventions that have driven this growth and the challenges that remain in achieving the full 500 GW target.
